speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: REPORTED ADJUSTMENT OF U.S. EXPORT SUBSIDY ON WHEAT
speechtext:
I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Agriculture. Would the minister care to comment
on the statement of Secretary of Agriculture Ezra Benson that the United States has been losing out in the Japanese market to Canadian wheat, and that as a result the United States has taken steps to adjust its export subsidy for wheat entering that market? Can the minister say whether this constitutes a threat to Canada's market for wheat in Japan and, if so, have representations been made to the United States?

maintopic: REPORTED ADJUSTMENT OF U.S. EXPORT SUBSIDY ON WHEAT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the Department of Agriculture has jurisdiction over the Canadian wheat board it keeps in very close touch with any statements made by our competitors. When the statement of Mr. Benson was reported in the press we immediately got in touch with official circles in Washington to make sure that we had the statement correctly. The statement was to the effect that Canadian wheat prices in the Japanese market were slightly lower than United States prices, and that Mr. Benson was considering action. Under the agreement arrived at between the ministers of the two countries it is understood there will be no change in marketing policies unless the other country is informed. Yesterday there was supposed to be a quarterly meeting of the officials and it was not held because of the snow storm in Washington. Therefore there has been no consultation. We are in close contact with the officials at Washington, and have asked that no action be taken without informing us in plenty of time to permit us to make representations.

speechtext: wish to direct a question to the Postmaster General. subsubtopic: DELIVERY OF CHRISTMAS CARDS FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think this is of more interest to Santa Claus than to Sir Galahad, but in either case we have been able to make more appropriate arrangements. Unlike Canada, where a 2-cent stamp will carry an unsealed Christmas card anywhere in the world, the United States has a rate of 3 cents for such cards to an address in their own country and 4 cents to Canada and other countries. This was a comparatively new rate in 1959, and many United States citizens placed only 3-cent stamps on their cards, including those for Canada. Those which could not be returned because of the absence of a return address were destroyed at that time by the United States post office rather than being forwarded to Canada.
This year, while the volume of such short-paid mail is not expected to be so heavy, we have had discussions with the United States postal authorities and they are going to forward these cards to Canada marked "postage due". In order to give Santa Claus and our heavily burdened letter carriers an assist, and since the postage already paid on such cards is 3 cents as against the 2-cent rate in Canada, it is not our intention in Canada to collect any additional amount when the cards are delivered by us.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-52, for the establishment of a national productivity council.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to speak at any length in moving this motion at this time. The situation has been fairly well covered, and there has been apparent general agreement as to the need for legislation such as that which is now before the house. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) made the opening speech in this connection. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) carried on during the committee stage on the resolution. I intend simply to deal in general with one or two phases of this matter.
The government is most anxious that this national productivity council should be established as soon as possible. What I intend to do, as I said a moment ago, is simply to deal in general with some of those matters that are peculiar to the council as envisaged by the bill in question.
It is of interest, of course, that the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Jung) brought to the attention of the house, at the last session, the general concept that is before the house today in the form of concrete legislation. As has already been said, the basic objectives of the British productivity council and those of the Canadian productivity council are the same. The Canadian council will, of course, be adapted so as best to meet Canadian needs.
The hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) suggested that there was some difference in the viewpoint I expressed on the occasion of the meeting in Ottawa when
Productivity Council
I convened and brought together representatives of industry, labour and the various other facets of the Canadian economy with a view to securing their views on those things which, in their opinion, might prove efficacious in meeting the employment situation in Canada.
It is of interest that similar ideas were advanced in the United States by both presidential candidates of the major parties. In other words, the success of the British productivity council and all others of like nature has been such that other nations have adopted a similar plan; and, as I said, in the United States the two leaders expressed views on this question that bore a striking resemblance to each other.
I convened the meeting of the various associations and groups by means of a letter dated September 28. The meeting was to be convened on October 4 and each of the organizations was asked to send one representative. The meeting duly took place. I do not know of any meeting that was ever more generally representative of all of Canada's economy in all its phases than the one in question.

Productivity Council
what I said on that occasion-and I think in general the press correctly reported the matter-I believe he will find that what I have stated is correct.
The basic objectives of the British productivity council, as I said, are approximately the same as those of the Canadian council. At this meeting, after various views were expressed by the representatives who attended, I suggested that there might be considered by those present a recommendation for the inauguration of a productivity council. While there was discussion on the matter and the details were not fully worked out, there was on the part of those present a unanimity in this regard. I hope there will be widespread support for the productivity council. The idea originated during the discussion, and the concept has been generally accepted.
The reason for setting up a Canadian productivity council is that concern has been expressed regarding the maintenance and expansion of productivity levels. These fears have been expressed by such bodies as the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, various labour organizations and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. As was said by the Minister of Labour, there has been an increasing awareness of the need to consider productivity from a long term view as well as from a short run view. Technological changes and productivity improvements have created short run unemployment problems and there is a need, as has been generally agreed, to stimulate productivity improvement.
We believe that through the formation of an independent national body, with its main representation drawn from industry and labour with some government participation, this body will encourage the development of suitable programs on a regional or national industry basis. Among its aims will be applied research in industry, the spreading and expansion of technical knowledge and experience, the development and promotion of ways and means whereby employment adjustments resulting from technological changes can be facilitated by individual employers through the stimulation of management and employee education and training.
Indeed, in the United States similar problems are being faced. In that connection I suggest an examination, without going into detail, of an article which recently appeared in the Christian Science Monitor, which sets forth the question regarding unemployment in the Morgan Guarantee survey, published by the Morgan Guarantee Trust Company of New York. That article is well worth reading. It sets forth the general reasons for the paradoxical phenomena of today, where with an increasing gross national product, with an

expanding economy, there is still unemployment. In the United States in the last few days it has been revealed that unemployment has been mounting very considerably, generally as the result of technological advance.
I might also say, in that connection, that the influence of technological advance and the contribution that it has made to unemployment was underlined and emphasized in an address given by Dr. Eugene Forsey on November 7, 1960, to the Ontario federation of labour. In that address he sets forth the situation that prevails in Canada, as in the United States, namely that there has been a very large increase in the number of employed. He points out that in Canada in 1948 the total number of people with jobs averaged about 4,690,000; in 1959 it averaged about 5,878,000, and in August of this year it reached an all-time high of 6,301,000. Then he goes on to say that even in September, after a drop of 132,000, the employment was still higher than it had ever been before except in August.
He goes on to outline the reasons for unemployment; the technological advances that have taken place, the shifts and changes in employment in various industries. I quote from what he said, because after all no one can say that he would be a prejudiced witness in any way in favour of the present government of Canada. He said:
I am convinced'-
I want to underline this, coming from him:
-that much of our unemployment results from technological change, or rather, from our failure to cope with technological change, to harness it, to make it do the job it could and should do. The evidence for this seems to me conclusive.
Then he points out the changes that have taken place:
First, agriculture. In 1946, people with jobs in agriculture numbered 1,186,000. Last year, the figure was 693,000. This year, it will probably be about 670,000.
Then he goes on. He is speaking here to the federation of labour and not to any political organization as such:
In 14 years, over half a million jobs have disappeared in this industry, nearly 44 per cent of the 1946 total.
He asks himself a question and then he answers that question:
Why? Because we are producing less? No. Because we can produce so much more with so many fewer people. Technological change, increased productivity: that's what did it.
Then he deals with the next phase of technological advance, manufacturing. These are his statistics in the course of this address:
In 1946, the number with jobs in manufacturing was about 1,222,000. Last year, it was 1,502,000... or an increase of 23 per cent.

Then he says that while there was an increase in manufacturing employment of about 23 per cent during that period, the gain in manufacturing production was about 75 per cent. Then he goes on to point out this fact, and all of this is of the essence when one discusses unemployment in Canada or in the United States, where the unemployment problem is almost identical with that in Canada. He says:
From 1947 to 1959 manufacturing production rose almost 60 per cent; manufacturing jobs rose only about 19 per cent.
Again he says that all of this is due to technological change:
[DOT]-for technological change has made it possible to produce more with fewer people.
Then he goes on and deals with other fields. I quoted from what he had said in this regard simply by way of indication that in this speech he does come to the heart of the problem which we face. He says:
Roughly speaking, last year the post-war gain in jobs in manufacturing, mining, forestry, fishing and trapping, and construction just about balanced the post-war loss in jobs in agriculture.
Then he says:
This is not something to lament. It is a triumph.
Then he proceeds to set out the facts in this regard:
Technological change is making extra people available, but the economies it produces are not producing enough jobs for them.
I shall say no more in this regard at the moment, except that he does point out the very great increase in the number of women workers. He says, and this is rather interesting too:
How can we solve these problems, notably the problems of organizing the hitherto almost unorgan-izable industries, of organizing women ...? I wish I knew. I don't.
I refer to what he said in this regard simply to indicate that this is a problem that requires to be attacked and met. Indeed, the problem today is one that has never been more challenging in Canada and the United States its effect is like that which followed the industrial revolution. I believe this council will be able to formulate programs to meet the problems created by automation and technological advance, and to meet the adjustments necessarily arising by reason of mechanical progress or obsolescence. It is going to be an effort of Canadians as a whole.
The membership has already been referred to during the course of the debate on the resolution. I expressed the hope that this body would bring together devoted citizens representative of business, labour, agriculture and all the various facets of Canadian development, with particular emphasis on
Productivity Council
representative women from business and professional clubs and the like and all other women's organizations, to consider this as a national problem and requiring and demanding the mobilization of the best thinking of Canadians as a whole. I would hope that the basic technique would be to direct the public consciousness not to fear but to faith; not to pointing out the difficulties without suggesting solutions, but to pointing to the strength and vigour of Canada and to bringing about, in a unity of effort, the best consideration that the best minds of Canada can bring to this problem.
As a result of the formation of this body I believe, indeed, that there will be the performance of a task which is as challenging as it is necessary to find a fulfilment. The initial task of the council and its staff will be to determine the general lines of approach appropriate under Canadian conditions. I would hope that the council would wish to consider establishing regional and area programs as well as programs for specific industries.
As to the field of endeavour, the branches of activity are generally set forth in the bill, though I am not allowed, of course, to refer to the clauses except in a general way. I might summarize clause 10 by saying that the purpose of this council will be the stimulation of industrial research, than which there is nothing more important in this country. Indeed, I express the hope that foreign concerns with subsidiaries in Canada will make available in Canada a major portion of the proportionate share that the Canadian industry bears to the total production of the entire industry and that this amount will be devoted to research rather than having the research done in another country, the course followed today. Further purposes of the council will include the dissemination of technical information, the improvement of production and distribution methods and the stimulation of training programs within industry at all levels.
Again, I find in Canada a situation similar to that which exists in the United States, a situation where many jobs cannot be filled because of the lack of technical training among the applicants. I shall not go into that question now because it has already been dealt with in the course of another debate. To continue, the purposes of the council will be to improve the promotion of efficient management methods and to encourage good human relations in industry. Nothing is more important than this particular field of human engineering. While today various government departments and agencies carry on informational, technical, research

Productivity Council
and other programs which would contribute to the council's work, much remains to be done in this connection. The objective of the council would be, in summary, greater industrial efficiency, more effective utilization of manpower, planned use of material and other resources to strengthen Canada's competitive position at home and abroad, and an increase in real income.
I do not think I shall say more at this time, except to indicate that the experience of other countries has pointed to action in this regard. I am not going to place before the house details of what has been done in Belgium and in other countries, except to say of their experience that much benefit has followed the adoption of this plan. This proposal is somewhat different from the British plan, inasmuch as the Canadian proposal makes provision for a measure of governmental participation. That is in line with the recommendations made in the United States setting up broad goals for the free economy, a purpose and objective that will rest upon this council.
I shall have more to say after the house has had the benefit of the opinions of hon. members in connection with this matter. I know we shall welcome any ideas or suggestions that may lead to any improvement in the bill, providing those suggestions are not of such a nature as would, in effect, constitute the council as a policy-making body with any control over the government. This, after all, would simply be applied socialism, and we, believing in private enterprise, will not accept suggestions of that type. But if there are views or ideas that will contribute to the strengthening of the objective and powers of the council or which in any way, in the opinion of the government, add to or strengthen the likelihood of attaining the objectives we have in mind, we shall be most happy to have the benefit of those ideas.
As I said a moment ago, the council will be widely representative of industry, commerce, agriculture and other primary industries. There will be representation from the workers and from the general public. In addition there will be four members who are officers or employees of Her Majesty's government employed in agencies of government which are active in dealing with the technical aspects of productivity. In this way we hope to strengthen the system as compared with that which exists in the United Kingdom, thereby making our contribution to the solution of the problem that faces both countries in North America today; a problem which has arisen in consequence of the vast improvement in technology in conjunction with

the tremendous competitive international warfare for trade which has been intensified in the last few years.
When the war was over, great nations found themselves devastated and industrially prostrate. Canada found easy markets everywhere in the world. That is past, today, and those countries which suffered most are now great industrial competitors. In addition to this competition there is rising competition from the communist countries which, generally speaking, will be intensified during the sixties.
That being so, countries believing in free enterprise will have to exercise their highest endeavours to assure the preservation of our standard of living and at the same time to maintain at the lowest possible minimum the costs of production. The achievement of both can be attained through the advances of technological skill. Concomitant with that we require to have the best opinion available about how to use technological advances not only for the attainment of those objectives but in order not to deny those who should have work the right and opportunity of having it.
That is the purpose of this legislation. It is a segment of the policy we are bringing before the house bill by bill. This policy, we believe, will be beneficial not only in the short term but in the longer term as well, and will provide the assurance of an ever-increasing expansion of the economy, an ever-increasing gross national product and an ever-increasing standard of living.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I in rising in my place for the first time extend my appreciation of the gallant expressions of welcome from many hon. members of this house on the occasion of my introduction, and in particular the gracious words of the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere (Mr. Paul) and the gracious gesture of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fairclough).
It might perhaps be forgiven if in rising in my place for the first time in this house I mention with affection my predecessor both in office and in this seat, whose untimely death we all regret. I knew the late W. L. Houck for most of my adult life and from the time of reaching my majority was one of his devoted supporters. His long years of selfless service to the people of his constituency, on municipal, provincial and federal levels, left a shining mark which few might hope to achieve. I know that his family and his constituents appreciate the many warm expressions of loss and of sympathy which emanated from many hon. members on his death.
It may also be understood if on this occasion I make some mention of the fine people of my constituency. They are Canadians of varied backgrounds, knit together by a common commitment to the future. They are of the best of Canada. They serve their nation both in peace and war and are among her proudest sons and daughters. It is a high duty to be called upon to serve them in the capacity of their federal representative.
This Christmas season will be an unhappy one in too many of the homes of Niagara because of accelerating lay-offs and discharges, failing businesses and a shrinking economy. I venture to suggest that none of them will find Christmas cheer for this year in the provisions of the bill before us.
The government made clear that this early session was not to deal with an economic emergency which it denies exists, but to deal with a heavy work load of legislation. Apparently the fruit on the legislative branches is so overripe that it must needs be plucked all at once. I point out that there is great need for legislation now to deal with the problems of the here and the now. Less than two months ago the right hon. gentleman opposite called together a conference of some 21 persons representing various Canadian groups in order to deal with unemployment. That subject appeared then to be of an emergency nature. I am unable to find how
Productivity Council
it has now ceased to be, with each monthly employment statistic more depressing than the last.
Following a day and a half of representations the Prime Minister announced the establishment of a productivity council, which has been embodied in a resolution and now in the bill before the house for consideration. The press reports of that day carried such headlines as "P.M. Pleased with Talks", "25-man Council to Plan More Jobs, P.M.'s Idea", "P.M.'s Solution: Productivity Council to Create Jobs". This was the impression created; yet I invite hon. members opposite to point out how the bill now before the house will create jobs or plan more jobs. How will it assist the people of my riding this winter? The Minister of Labour last evening, as reported at page 733 of Hansard, tacitly admitted that it will not do so when he said:
In some fields the results will appear fairly soon. In more complex fields it will take longer.
I invite hon. members of the government to tell us in what field there will be results fairly soon, and to tell us what the government means by "fairly soon".
The minister sponsoring this bill indicated that the proposed council is to be modelled after the British productivity council. Has the minister or the government heretofore consulted any officials of the British productivity council directly? Has there been any consultation with the productivity councils in Japan and Lebanon, to which he referred? Surely these were set up to deal with problems similar to British problems and exportable to those countries because of the similar nature of those problems. The British council was set up to spread ideas of industrial efficiency throughout British industry and to meet shortages in order to shift from a wartime to a peacetime economy, to produce sufficient goods to fill both export and domestic markets.
That is very different from that situation which now obtains in Canada. We need markets now for what we produce now, and we need expansion of that production to create new jobs to put to work our expanding labour force. There was in England at the time of the setting up of this council no question at all of unemployment. There was full employment, but even with the labour force all at work the British did not have goods to sell to their own people.
Surely it cannot be argued that increased productivity alone necessarily means expanded ready markets. We have before us the example of the tremendous increase in productivity of the Canadian agricultural community. The Prime Minister today referred to certain figures with respect to this, showing that in 14 years some 44 per cent of

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: I, too, approve of those remarks, and if the government will only do so it may claim the support not only of all hon. members but of the country as a whole.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of pleasure that I extend my congratulations to the lady member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh) on the quality of her maiden speech. It showed thorough preparation, a thoughtful assessment of the situation and a very deep concern for her constituents who are unemployed and are seeking some remedy through legislation introduced by the government. The hon. member for Niagara Falls, Mr. Speaker, is a colourful addition to, except in a few cases, a somewhat drab political landscape.
I now wish to congratulate the Prime Minister on his excellent presentation of his Christmas present to the Canadian people, a present well wrapped in the ribbons of language and eloquence; and, Mr. Speaker, I certainly love to watch the Prime Minister waving in the wind of his own eloquence.
Productivity Council
However, after listening very carefully to the speech by the minister at the resolution stage and the speech by the Prime Minister this afternoon, I am afraid that the Christmas present is mostly wrapping and ribbon and there is very little in the box.
While we in this group will admit that there may be some value in this productivity council in so far as it provides for research and the obtaining of facts, and also for a better understanding of our economic problems by a greater number of people, we do question the effectiveness of the bill to meet the problems that we face in Canada now.
We do so on two grounds, Mr. Speaker. First of all, the productivity council has to work within the framework of an economic philosophy and circumstances which from our point of view-I am speaking as a democratic socialist and proud of it; I am an unregenerate socialist, and I say that without any hesitation -practically defeat the objects and purpose of the council. Where do we find unemployment today? On the North American continent, in the United States and Canada, in two countries with abundant natural resources and tremendous opportunities for all their people to have a high standard of living.
There is no question but that this is a most serious problem. Anyone who listened to the debates on television between the two candidates for the presidency of the United States will realize that the problem concerns the government and people of the United States. What concerns me is that while the great percentage of the people in the United States and Canada are enjoying a reasonable standard of living and in some cases a considerable measure of prosperity, we have this hard core of unemployment at the same time, which we see little opportunity to decrease at present.
The cycle is now complete, Mr. Speaker. Here are nations that can co-operate for military purposes, for defensive purposes; yet in the world of today they are cutting one another's throats economically. That is one of the first things to which we have to give consideration. We combine for defensive purposes, and at the same time we compete with one another for the vanishing markets in the world today. That situation will continue, in the opinion of the members of this group, until we are wise enough to recognize that we can only treat the world as a whole at the present time and try to take advantage of markets that are closed to us because of the foreign policy of our neighbour and other states.
I said that we criticize the bill on two grounds. First of all we as socialists criticize it because we believe that, with the best of intentions, the productivity council will be

Productivity Council
working within the framework of an economic order and philosophy that defeats the very purpose and objects of the council. There is no suggestion in the bill for a program of over-all planning of production. There is no suggestion in the bill that there should be any consideration of fiscal policy, which is a most important aspect of economic policy. There is no suggestion in the bill that the council will give consideration to a national investment policy, possibly a guided or directed investment policy. There is no suggestion in the bill that this council should draft a program or make recommendations for full employment in the days ahead.
I am not suggesting that these things can be done overnight. There is no suggestion that this council should interfere in any way with what I would term a free reign and a free rein enterprise system. Admitting the best of intentions on the part of the Prime Minister and the government, we doubt the effectiveness of this productivity council under our present circumstances.
Second, we doubt its effectiveness because there is no power in the bill for this council to make recommendations, but only to report to parliament. According to the language of the bill, it may do this and that. With respect to many important aspects it does not say "shall" but rather says "may". We criticize this legislation on that ground.
When we look at the measure we also find that the council is a charitable organization. I can well understand the reason for defining this as a charitable organization if it intends to receive gifts and so on from individuals, organizations or other sources. Just think of it, Mr. Speaker; we are aiming to solve our economic problems by establishing a charitable organization in Canada. There may be a lot of misunderstanding about that point, but anyone who reads the bill very carefully and gives the matter some consideration will notice that this is a charitable organization being established by the government of Canada to meet a very serious situation in our country at this time.
I listened, as I always do, with great interest to the Prime Minister. When he was speaking I noticed that he said that this productivity council would be an independent national body, and he made some reference to the productivity councils in Great Britain and other countries. I agree with what I thought was a very good point made by the hon. member for Niagara Falls. You cannot compare the operations of productivity councils in countries like Great Britain and the other countries that were mentioned with the possibilities for a productivity council of this type in Canada. Our major economic problem so far as overseas markets are concerned is

the export of primary agricultural and industrial products, and this presents a different situation entirely from our point of view.
The Prime Minister also said that the council was going to be formed to mitigate the effects of technological changes. When I listen to the Prime Minister I listen to the words he uses, because sometimes in a single word you will find illustrated a frame of mind, an approach that actually is not revealed in the development of his speech or in the development of his argument. He said that the purpose was to mitigate the effects of technological changes. What does the word "mitigate" mean? It means to moderate, to appease, to alleviate, but not to cure. We in this group want to see this government take some action along the road to curing this chronic unemployment situation. We do not for one moment say it is going to be done overnight. However, we want to see a course of action that will offer hope in the years immediately ahead for some solution to this question, and not merely a mitigation of the effects of technological changes and improvements.
In concluding his remarks the Prime Minister made reference to an expanding economy and a higher standard of living. The situation we face at the present time is this. While this body is termed a productivity council, it is the same old story. The farmers and the workers of Canada produce too much and consequently they are unemployed. It is not only a question of productivity; it is a question of distribution and of markets, and those matters are related to the policies I have mentioned.
Therefore, in concluding my brief remarks on second reading of this bill, I say that we question the effectiveness of this measure for the reasons I have outlined this afternoon.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make some brief comments on Bill No. C-52 which is before us at this moment. This most important measure is one which, in my opinion, has captured great interest throughout our country. We have heard this afternoon three most interesting speeches on this matter. I feel that the speech of the Prime Minister was a most powerful exposition of the bill that is before us, and explained in great measure the hopes and ideas as to the future part this council might play in our country.
I think we were all pleased as well to hear the stimulating and interesting speech of the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh). In this, her first speech in the House of Commons, she certainly presented her ideas in an interesting fashion. Among her remarks I noted the thought expressed -and I believe this statement was made the

other evening as well by the hon. member lor Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith)-that we should perhaps not connect too closely the British productivity council with the council we propose to establish in Canada. I can only say that it would seem amiss indeed if our government did not compare our proposed new council to some extent with similar bodies in other countries around the world. It would be most amazing if we did not do that.
The hon. member for Niagara Falls made remarks to the effect that the British council was established to make more goods available, and that there was no problem of unemployment at that time; she continued that we had a reverse problem here in Canada. We have many goods to market but we have an unemployment problem. We have men and women left over, so to speak. It seems to me that surely these two matters, even if we admit to the basic truth of them, are not far apart at all. It seems to me that the crucial problem in Canada in order to make more jobs is to do things better, more cheaply and faster, and that this process in turn will make for more employment; and that this thought in turn is partly the responsibility, the idea and the reasoning behind the productivity council we have in mind.
Of course these two plans are not so far apart. The plan or purpose of the British productivity council is not so far apart at all from that of the council we now have in mind. The hon. member for Niagara Falls went on to suggest that technological progress in Canada can make for unemployment, and decried technology on that basis. To me this suggestion seems to be an example of retrograde thinking. Indeed, it seems to me that we need to sell more, to make things more cheaply, more rapidly and in better quality. This is the key in the long run, and indeed in the short run, to more employment and more sales throughout Canada and outside our country as well.
I do not think this voicing of opinion on the part of the hon. lady is compatible with the extremely progressive constituency from which she comes. I believe it is much more compatible with the ideas and the thinking, rigid and inflexible as it is, of the party into which she has fallen.
I noted the other evening the remarks of the hon. member for Ottawa West. At one stage he said that the Liberal party had voiced support in this house of measures and ideas of a similar nature. He mentioned that last spring, the idea really was that of the opposition Liberal party. No mention was made, of course, of what the hon. member for Vancouver Centre said or the ideas voiced by him at an earlier stage in this house. The
Productivity Council
hon. member for Ottawa West went on to say that this idea of a productivity council was really based on the 1958 campaign platform of the Liberal party. He added that it actually came from something called the Pearson plan, supplemented and bolstered by visions of the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). He was really giving most grudging approval to the measure before the house. It was approval, but it was given in inches and fractions of inches; it was approval in most minute amounts.
It seems to us on this side of the house, that opposition may have at least a partially salutary effect on the Liberal party. However, it puzzles us-and this is something that has been said before-how it happens that after a generation of forming the government in this country, these new ideas have actually popped up from the other side of the house only when their party is in opposition; and that after a generation of having authority to bring in new measures of this sort, we see them now giving grudging approval to the many new plans that we have brought forward in the last few weeks and months.
As to the idea of productivity itself, may I say that it is one which has been perhaps loosely defined by various bodies. It is an idea which is perhaps difficult to measure in terms of figures and in terms of what various groups and various people think or wish to call it. I believe that one of the purposes of our new council would be perhaps to devise some definitive means of explaining what productivity figures really are. Since I have come to this house-and I am sure many other members are faced with the same difficulty-I have read many varying and contradictory remarks about productivity. They come from labour organizations, manufacturing organizations and various groups which may have rather different objectives than mine. I would hope this new council would have as one of its purposes some measure of ability to give really definitive figures as to productivity in various industries and various types of activity throughout our country.
Productivity has been defined as well in various reports. One of them, the so-called Gordon commission report, has an interesting chapter on this subject and discusses it in some detail. It refers to productivity as the ratio of total input to output, and goes on to discuss the relationship of labour to these figures. The gross domestic product of any given industry in a year may be regarded as the output, and the input the number of man hours employed in that industry in the year in question, with no distinction made between regular hours and overtime hours. These are some of the methods and terms by which productivity may be compared and examined.

Productivity Council
In other words, we are really talking about gross domestic production per man hour. Perhaps this is the wisest explanation for our term "productivity".
Why do we say that the productivity is important in Canada? This is perhaps an obvious question, and the answers are equally obvious. We are a country of tremendous importing and exporting needs and capabilities. In a country as small as Canada, with our ribbon-like population and our tremendous distribution areas, productivity must be a keystone to a healthy and successful economy. It seems to me that in Canada productivity really must mean efficiency; it must mean efficient production. In other words, efficiency must be almost synonymous with the term "productivity". We need productivity in our internal markets. We are faced today with a tremendous challenge of imported goods from Britain, Europe and Asia. I think that challenge will grow and will not diminish in the immediate years ahead. The tremendous necessity that we have for these goods is one of the reasons productivity is so important to Canada.
I have mentioned that we have a small population. We have tremendous distribution costs. All these things make for a large overhead in Canada. Indeed, if we are faced, as we sometimes are, by restrictions imposed by other countries on the incoming of our manufactured and other goods, and if we must depend entirely on a local or domestic Canadian market, our overhead may indeed be large and fixed and very difficult for many Canadian manufacturers and people in other businesses to work under.
The United States, for example, a neighbour of ours, has a rather different problem. Their dependence on exports and imports is perhaps roughly one tenth of ours, a factor something like the population ratio between our two countries. Their tremendous population and perhaps little greater distribution costs make for an overhead that is not comparable to that faced by many Canadian businessmen.
Mr. Speaker, what makes for greater productivity in Canada? The Prime Minister has stated previously that we have seen a resurgence in the war torn countries of western Europe, and indeed Japan, into the commercial markets of the world. I might say that in a strange sense productivity may be brought about by wars. This is a horrible thing, but we have seen increased productivity arise as a secondary effect of terrible and destructive wars. I believe we have seen this in some countries of western Europe. I believe it is the consensus of economists that certain countries which did not suffer such

terrible ravages of their homelands and industries have more troubles today, perhaps, in their industries than there are in the industries of other countries which were more completely razed by the war.
We have seen a period of resurgence in Germany through the compulsion of the times and the facts of life. Germany had to rebuild much of her basic industry from the ground up. This terrible toll was paid, in a sense; and a decade or 15 years later, through her dependence on new plants, new machinery and new ideas, that country and other countries like her-perhaps Japan is an example -have been put on a competitive or superior footing with other countries of western Europe and, indeed, with ourselves here in North America. War is a terrible thing, but it has a secondary effect and a very direct effect on the productivity of a country in the years that follow.
Other things, of course, make for productivity. The strenuous competition that is facing us in Canada today might be said to be the very lifeblood of productivity. Competition must force increased productivity, and this is really what we are facing in Canada today.
The Liberal party talks about technology and how increased technology would result in more unemployment. I say we need increased technology, and we need a great deal of it.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: When did the Liberal party ever say that?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
The competition we are facing in Canada today is forcing our hand. We must become more competitive; we must trade more. The brilliant trade conference now taking place is an example of the resolution and determination of this government to sell more products in more markets all around the world.
Technical education, the aid to technical schools which has recently been discussed in this house, and measures of this sort must be part of the solution to unemployment, efficiency and productivity in our country. The technical skills of our workers will indeed affect our production. In addition, all the improvements in medical standards and physical well-being that have gone on in recent years affect our productivity in Canada, in the same sense.
Mental well-being, the tensions of our modern life, might be placed on the other side. These tensions may have a deleterious effect on productivity and the mental wellbeing of some, at least, of our workers and our management staff. The fewer hours worked by labour today may affect productivity. It certainly gives many people in

many walks of life throughout Canada more opportunity to indulge in outside interests and activities. One could only hope, from the point of view of productivity, that this shortening of working hours and the very general increase in wage rates would also be followed by a corresponding increase in responsibility and interest in the job at hand.
This is something which I think is a fundamental worry to many of us, that decreased working hours and increased wages ought to be followed by an increased interest and skill in the job to be done, in the job at hand. To me this is also part and parcel of our productivity needs in Canada. Labour-management harmony throughout our country, the incidence of strikes and disagreements between opposing factions, must necessarily affect our productivity. The interest of the workers can affect their efficiency in any given job. The psychological effects of strife must be adverse indeed to production within our economy. The desire to do a job well, rather than to earn the maximum for a minimum of hours and effort, must affect our efficiency and our productivity.
These are perhaps some areas, you might say some shadowy areas, that are most difficult to legislate upon, naturally. Nevertheless they are fundamental in what I say is necessary in Canada; that is, increased efficiency, the ability to make goods better and cheaper. The skills and attitudes of the workers affect productivity, of course, in any country; and that productivity is measured by the resources, the capital and tools and the management, if you will, that go into different industries such as agriculture and others in our country. We have seen-we know, because the figures show us-that productivity is frequently highest in a number of basic resource industries in Canada such as mining, oil and gas, in which large volumes of valuable products may be handled at times by few men and with large capital investments. Nevertheless, a complicating factor within our country has been our problem of distribution, the fact that in the past at least a great deal of capital has had to go for the exploitation or development of these basic industries, and this might not have been the case in other countries. Thus much of our basic capital, while developing our primary industries to a state of high productivity, has had to go as well to the actual tying or holding of this country together through railroads or other basic forms of communication just to maintain ourselves as a unit. The incidence of the inflow of capital from Britain, the United States and elsewhere has tended to markedly
Productivity Council
affect our productivity in the past. There have been periods when this inflow of capital has been great, followed by other periods of levelling off in which the effect of the inflow of large sums of capital was felt as business progressed and the worth-while and profitmaking results of this capital were felt by the investors.
Productivity in Canada is measured through education and research. These must be keystones of increased productivity and efficiency in our country. Education is a keystone-and I am sure this council will play a part in this-to establishing relations between labour and management; to a knowledge of how technology may disturb, in any given instance, the labour relationship in any particular industry; how this in the long run may have a beneficial effect on the price of goods and on the increased markets resulting from that, and on the increased jobs in service and other industries which labour may be able to gain. Thus education and harmony among the various parties increases productivity and efficiency in our country. This sort of liaison education would, I would think, be of fundamental concern to this new council.
We discuss automation. We talk of automation, this process by which a series of mechanical jobs may be joined together, which is looked upon with distress by some and favour by others. Automation is particularly evident in a number of our basic industrial fields, in oil and so forth and, indeed, in government in the mailing of numbers of cheques in welfare and social security programs. Here again automation plays its part to an increasing extent.
I was interested just the other day in an example of automation coming into our government. It seems there are some 100 people involved in a certain branch of the dominion bureau of statistics analysing, largely by hand, the returns and papers from the various customs ports across Canada. The bureau has planned the installation of machinery to do this, at least in part, mechanically. Here is an example of the way in which automation might displace, at least momentarily, some of these people; yet I have instance after instance in which manufacturing concerns in Canada seeking the establishment of new industries, dependent upon the availability of fast, accurate and full information from the bureau of statistics, find themselves enormously helped by the possession of more up to date statistical information. Here are new industries which depend on the availability and accuracy of this information and which will be served even better by automation, as a result of which we will have new jobs and new industries in Canada. So on

Productivity Council
the one hand we see some disappearance of employment, but on the other hand there is, I think, a very much larger benefit from the increased employment possibilities throughout the whole of our country.
Agriculture has been mentioned during this debate by a number of speakers, and while productivity in agriculture is not generally regarded as being as high as it is in the business sector of our country, the rate of increase in productivity in agriculture in Canada has been, in the past number of years at least, much more rapid. Productivity in the field of agriculture has indeed been most extraordinary. We can look at the chicken broiler business, the dairying field, as well as many other fields and see a fantastic increase in efficiency and productivity. This is demonstrated also by the increase in size of the average farm, as well as by the perplexing and somewhat troubling decline in the number of agricultural workers.
The increase in the total production of farm products here in North America has certainly been a bit of a paradox in the face of the cries of warning and dire predictions by economists and others who have been saying through many of the past years that we would run out of our food supplies. In spite of those predictions our production in agriculture has always increased at a more rapid rate than our population. In my mind I see no cessation to that rate of increase, and no ceiling to the possibility of future productivity in agriculture in North America.
Productivity in the business sector of the economy increases to the extent of 2 per cent, 2J per cent or 3 per cent a year. In agriculture the increase has tended to be somewhat greater. The Gordon commission has made some predictions until the year 1970 or 1980. Other bodies in Canada have done similar things. Mr. Speaker, we have reached a turning point in our economic or social life and must search for new formulas and by-words. We must reconsider our economic theory in relation to our present difficulties, try to improve it or to discover a new one in line with our needs, our way of thinking and our situation.
Our guiding motives, if we want to achieve a prosperous and expanding economy, must converge on means to raise our national production, while improving the standard of living of all our citizens. That is the source of the problem of wages or of labour management relations to which economists have been unable to find an adequate answer.
Under the present economic concept, management strives, as duty commands them to to, to safeguard the capital invested in an industry. They aim at maximum profits, which is a legitimate goal.
The worker, on the other hand, must do an honest job for the benefit of his employer and society. He therefore seeks to get better wages for the shortest possible working hours, and that too is legitimate.
However, between the two groups, conflicts arise which can only be harmful to the economy of the country as a whole. Now according to the Rev. Bernard Dempsey, conflicts between capital and labour are only two economic factors and have no human element.
Why are humans incapable, or I might say unwilling, to control those two factors?
Is it that employers and workers are so concerned about materialism that they ignore social and spiritual values?
Recently, at a meeting of the Canadian Labour Congress, Cardinal Leger said:
Economy cannot ignore morals. That estrangement of morals from economy has led to two equally materialistic modern economic systems: economic liberalism and marxist communism.
Admittedly, in the light of past experience in industrial relations, for some years we have not been making any progress towards a permanent solution. Our record is one of repeated failures.

Productivity Council
Why, then, is it so difficult to come upon the magic formula that would offer the possibilities of peace?
Why is it that, in any conflict, humans have to grasp desperately at a major part of the spoils, when they could be divided up fairly and peacefully?
It is not my intention to apportion blame as between employers and workers, for in my opinion, their mistakes balance out.
If no such magic formula has been found, it is because neither employers nor employees have looked for the solution, or else have ignored the difficulties.
Through the years, several economic theories have been evolved and tried out, and with altogether conflicting results.
Adam Smith had a theory which was further developed by Ricardo. That theory had unfortunate implications for mankind and it was called "the iron law on wages", which implied that a certain portion of mankind was bound to live under bare survival standards.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker,
I was referring to the various economic theories which were developed a number of years ago, and I mentioned those of Adam Smith and Ricardo.
Later on, two economists were impressed by the inhuman aspect of such a wage theory, and developed a theory which took human needs into account. One of them was Marx, who found a solution to the wage problem. His theory was quite simple. It abolished private property and made the state politically responsible for the production and

distribution of goods. Unfortunately, his system has led men to sacrifice their freedom and justice, both in the political and economic spheres.
For nearly 50 years now, freedom loving and justice loving countries have been fighting this theory which has been condemned by the popes and by the whole democratic world.
The other man who tried to find a solution to the wage problem was the German Von Thunen. He based his theory on the right to private ownership, and tried to settle the problem without any political interference.
His theory is expressed in the fair wage formula. Here is how it applies: in an expanding economy, every person, apart from satisfying his subsistance needs, must share in the general prosperity. This is called the theory of "profit sharing".
To illustrate Von Thunen's thesis, I should like to describe his experiment in the field of land cultivation in Germany, around 1800.
On the basis of his theory, he distributed part of the profits every year to each of his workers. The ratio was based on his own personal formula. At the end of the year, instead of paying the worker's share in cash, he reinvested it in the business, and the following year, he paid out a given cash interest.
Over the years, the money in the fund increased, and the annual interest payments to the workers also rose.
At the end of his career, the worker was entitled to an amount large enough to allow him to retire.
The plan was a success over several generations, and it is on the basis of the same principles that are organized the 30,000 American industries, as well as a number of Canadian industries, which apply the theory of profit sharing.
Of those two theories, that of Marx denies justice and individual freedom, while the other, that of Von Thunen, is based on the freedom of man and takes due account of his needs, without any political interference.
Mr. Speaker, if we analyse the results of our present economic system over the past 50 years, we find that we have always been faced with the problem of wages versus capital.
As our technological and scientific methods helped to bring about an increased production, the resulting distribution, in view of our present concept of wages, became more and more unrealistic.
Productivity Council
In order to maintain our economy in a state of progress and to enable the world to use the products created by technological progress, we have had to keep raising wages.
Then, credit facilities developed to such an extent and so rapidly that they now threaten to smother economic life.
To react against the purchasing power created by these credit facilities, governments have taxed goods and then levied personal and corporation income tax. Later on came social assistance programs and fringe benefits were added to wages.
In spite of all our efforts the application of these policies has not solved the economic problems that originate with capital and wages.
There is always more inflation and high production costs are keeping us out of international markets.
Under the guidance of economists in many cases, authorities keep trying out certain theories through which we are gradually being led to government control over our economic system.
When that stage is reached, we will be wondering what difference there is between the socialist or communist system and ours, apart from our political climate, which will be less despotic and probably more enlightened.
There are two solutions to our economic problems. The first one, which was preached by Marx does away with private property and limits freedom, since the whole of the economy is placed under state control. The other, developed by Von Thunen, maintains private property and freedom within the framework of governmental legislation which affects economic life but not political life.
It is urgent that we start considering this latter theory and try to adapt it to our own society.
The application of that profit sharing theory would be to the advantage of our economy. It should, however, become a national economic policy enforced not through government decree but by private enterprise with the support of the government.
What is that profit sharing theory?
Several organizations have given a definition of it, but let me quote only one, which, in my opinion, is the best. This is a definition taken from "The Profit Sharing Industries, 1957". It reads as follows:
(Text):
Any procedure under which an employer pays or makes available to all regular employees subject

to reasonable eligibility rules, in addition to prevailing rates of pay, special current or deferred sums based on the profits of the business.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-5, to amend the National Energy Board Act (drainage works).
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill seeks to amend the National Energy Board Act by including in it section 273 of the Railway Act. When the National Energy Board Act was passed first in 1959, some 40 sections of the Railway Act, sections 207 to 246 inclusive and section 248, were included in the National Energy Board Act but section 273 which had

been included in the Pipe Lines Act, which preceded and was replaced by the National Energy Board Act, was omitted.
We have two sets of rules governing pipe lines. At least that is the situation in southwestern Ontario. I think it is reasonable to assume that the drainage laws of the various provinces would be similar. There are in Canada only two areas in which pipe lines have seriously interfered with drainage or caused problems in connection with drainage so far. These areas may be increased in number as the number of pipe lines across the country is increased. However, at the present time the only areas seriously affected are southwestern Ontario and the lower Fraser valley in British Columbia.
In southwestern Ontario we have two sets of laws or rules governing pipe lines. The pipe lines which operate under provincial charter come under provincial drainage laws. They come under the jurisdiction of the municipal drainage law and they are compelled to pay any extra costs which arise in connection with a drain by reason of their presence or operation. However, pipe lines operating under federal charter do not come under provincial drainage laws. They come under the national energy board and thus far they have not been compelled to pay the extra costs to drainage schemes which arise by their presence or operation. In time this situation may be changed but at the present time pipe lines operating under federal jurisdiction or at least the one running through our area which operates under federal jurisdiction, have been carrying on under much more advantageous rules than have the pipe lines which operate under provincial jurisdiction.
This amendment would make pipe lines operating under federal charter subject to provincial drainage laws in the same way as are pipe lines which operate under provincial charter. Pipe lines involved in municipal drainage schemes would be treated like any other property owner. They would be subject to assessment for benefit cost or damage like other properties and their owners would enjoy the right of appeal to county or district courts for adjustment in such assessments. Owners of pipe lines would be made responsible for any added cost to a municipal drainage scheme caused by their presence.
The provisions contained in the proposed amendment would include in the National Energy Board Act section 273 of the Railway Act which was incorporated in the Railway Act in 1903 after an extended debate in parliament. It has been suggested that the arguments which were valid and successful in connection with drainage problems caused
National Energy Board Act by the railways in 1903 are equally valid today in connection with pipe lines.
In order to indicate that this bill has considerable support, may I point out at this time that this proposed amendment is endorsed by the association of Ontario land surveyors; the Middlesex county council; the chairman of the special committee of the Ontario legislature which was set up to inquire into land expropriation proceedings in Ontario; the townships of East Williams and London and the Ontario federation of agriculture.
It may be worth while at this stage to explain briefly to those who are not familiar with the subject how drainage is carried out in the areas of greater rainfall in Canada, especially in southwestern Ontario and in the lower Fraser valley of British Columbia.
Tile drainage of farm land in some parts of Canada is essential to successful crop production. In wet seasons in Canada's areas of greater rainfall surplus water gathers in the low spots on the farm fields. This surplus water interferes with cultivation and also ruins standing crops. Tile drainage is the best cure for this condition. Proper drainage permits aeration of the soil and promotes the healthy growth of crops. Drainage also facilitates cultivation of the soil.
In some areas of southwestern Ontario on level farms it has been found necessary to construct parallel lines of tile drains across the entire farm as close together as 15 yards. Tile drainage is accomplished by burying clay tile end to end in a trench approximately two feet below the surface of the land. When the land becomes saturated with water the extra water seeps into the drain between the ends of the tile and is carried away to a suitable outlet. It is essential that a drain maintain a steady downward grade-or, as we might say, a downward slope-from its upper end to its outlet. Water cannot run uphill. When anything obstructs a drain or the grade of a drain or the downward slope, it causes a pocket or a stagnant pool within the drain and the sediment settles there and plugs the drain. I repeat that it is essential that the downward slope or grade of a drain must be constant from its upper reaches to its outlet.
We might liken a drain system to a tree. Starting at the trunk the tree spreads out into the main branches. These in turn spread out into smaller branches and you end up on the outer fringes of the tree with the twigs or extremely small branches. A drain would be described in the inverse order. You would start at the outer end of the drain with the small branches or twigs, as it were. These small branches flow into the larger branches and they in turn flow into the main branches
764	HOUSE OF
National Energy Board Act which in turn flow into the trunk. Carrying the description a step further may I say that at these outer fringes of a drain you would commence with tile four inches in diameter. As these bring the water together into the larger drains it is necessary to increase the size of the tile to a diameter of six, eight or ten inches, up to 12 inches and sometimes even larger. When you get so far down the drain that a tile is no longer sufficient to carry the volume of water, then for the rest of the drain you must use an open ditch.
You have trouble if a pipe line goes across the country and is not buried deep enough in the soil so that the drains can cross above the pipe line. The only cure is to lower the pipe line. You can well imagine that with a 10, 12 or even up to a 30 inch pipe line, that this becomes a very costly business.
You cannot lower just a short length of the pipe line; you have to dig the dirt from under the pipe line for hundreds of yards back on either side and lay down a whole long section of that pipe line into the soil. It is necessary to get the earth out from below it and allow the pipe line to settle under its own weight. Later I will give specific instances of where this has been done, and the cost.
Most drainage is organized and carried out by municipal drainage authorities. Farmers may construct short drains on their own where they have a suitable outlet, but as a rule it is necessary for all the farmers living in a watershed, or part of a watershed, to join together to construct a drain. This is done under the municipal drainage act.
When a majority of farmers feel a drain is required in a certain area a petition is circulated under the provisions of the municipal drainage act. The municipal council has no alternative, when it receives a petition signed by a majority of ratepayers, but to establish the drain. An engineer is called in. He makes a survey, and not only does he lay out the plan of the physical drain but it is his responsibility to prepare an estimate of the cost and make an assessment on every property owner toward the cost of the drain according to the benefit each property owner receives from it.
Under the Ontario municipal drainage act, which applies to those pipe lines that come under provincial charter, pipe lines companies are treated the same as any other property owner in a drainage scheme. They are assessed for benefit or allowed damages the same as any other property owner. All the litigation is carried on at the municipal level. An appeal is taken to the county court involved. That is the way the local people like it. In addition to that, the pipe line company is compelled, under provincial law, under 

the municipal drainage act, to pay any added costs which accrue to the drain because of the presence or operation of the pipe line.
Perhaps I may for a moment make a brief review of the history of section 273 of the Railway Act, which it is suggested should be incorporated in the National Energy Board Act. In the early years of the century railways sometimes proved to be serious obstacles to the construction of drains. Farmers and municipalities often experienced difficulty in arranging with railways for crossing rights. Farmers or drainage authorities who wished to carry a drain across a railway had in those days to apply to the railway committee of the privy council for an order for crossing.
This railway committee of the privy council was the antecedent of the board of transport commissioners. The problems met by farmers and drainage authorities in their dealings with the railway committee of the privy council were fully outlined in the House of Commons debates of June 16, 1903 by Messrs. Cowan of South Essex, Sutherland of North Essex, McCarthy of North Simcoe, Lennox of South Simcoe, Lancaster of Lincoln and Niagara, Demers of St. Jean-Iber-ville and others of that parliament.
It was contended by those members in 1903 that although the railway committee of the privy council had done everything in its power to make an adjudication on drainage crossing applications as convenient and inexpensive as possible, farmers and municipal authorities were very reluctant to apply to the railway committee because they feared the cost of litigation before the railway committee would be more than they could afford. They preferred to get along without the drainage rather than take the chance of running into heavy expenses.
The railway committee often sent out engineers to conduct hearings in the field, but the farmers still feared the costs. The same reluctance on the part of farmers and municipal authorities to apply to a central agency, such as the national energy board, still persists. Local authorities prefer to have this litigation brought to the local or municipal level, as it is brought under the provincial drainage laws in Ontario. Parliament remedied the situation in 1903 by incorporating section 273 into the Railway Act. This section makes railways subject to provincial drainage law. It brought the litigation to the municipal level and made railways responsible for the added cost to a drainage scheme brought about by the presence or operation of a railway.
For many years the railways were the only public utilities which created problems of this nature. We now have gas and oil pipe

lines and other utilities creating similar drainage problems. The Pipe Lines Act was enacted by parliament some years ago to control interprovincial and international oil and gas pipe lines. As with the railways, control was entrusted to the board of transport commissioners. Many provisions of the Railway Act were made applicable to pipe lines, including entry upon, use and expropriation of lands. However, section 273 of the Railway Act, to apply provincial drainage laws to pipe lines companies, was not incorporated. Instead, the board of transport commissioners was given authority over drain rights of way that crossed interprovincial or international pipe lines. This section 32 was carried forward, except for non-material changes, into the National Energy Board Act as section 77. Section 77 of the National Energy Board Act reads as follows:
77 (1) A highway, private road, railway, irrigation ditch, drain, telegram, telephone line or a line for the transmission of hydrocarbons, power or any other substance may, by leave of the board, be carried across any pipe line and for such purposes may be constructed upon, along, under or across such pipe line.
(2)	Upon application for leave, the board may grant the application in whole or in part and upon such terms and conditions as the board considers proper.
That is the part of the National Energy Board Act which controls drainage problems in southwestern Ontario at the present time. The result of the present laws is that the railway utilities both interprovincial and provincial, and the provincial pipe lines utilities, are subject to provincial drainage authorities while the interprovincial and international pipe line utilities are subject to the national energy board.
It is requested, therefore, that steps be taken to incorporate the municipal drainage laws in the National Energy Board Act so as to apply these laws to interprovincial and international pipe lines. This may be done as suggested by including Section 273 of the Railway Act with the other sections of the Railway Act which are incorporated into section 75(1) of the National Energy Board Act.
Section 75(1) of the National Energy Board Act now reads:
Sections 207 and 246 and 248 of the Railway Act in so far as they are reasonably applicable and not inconsistent with this act, apply mutatis mutandis to companies and their works and undertakings.
The suggested amendment would cause it to read:
Sections 207 and 246, section 248 and section 273 of the Railway Act in so far as they are reasonably applicable and not inconsistent with this act, apply mutatis mutandis to companies and their works and undertakings.
National Energy Board Act
Just what is this section 273 of the Railway Act? It contains five subsections, the first of which reads as follows:
(1)	Whenever by virtue of any act of any province through which the railway runs, proceedings may be had or taken by any municipality or landowner for any drainage, or drainage works, upon and across the property of any other landowner in such province, the like proceedings may, at the option of such municipality or landowner, be had or taken by such municipality or landowner for drainage or drainage works, upon and across the railway and lands of the company, in the place of the proceedings before the board, provided in Section 272.
Turned into layman's language I would interpret this to mean that railway companies are made liable like any other property owner in a municipal drainage scheme. They are subject to the same responsibility as to assessment for benefit or damage and for their share of the costs of a drain. They are subject to the law at the municipal level. Appeals would be heard by a county court.
Subsection (2) provides:
(2)	In case of any such proceedings, the drainage laws of the province, subject to any previous order or direction of the board made or given with respect to drainage of the same lands, apply to the lands of the company upon or across which such drainage is required, to the same extent as to the lands of any land owner of such province; but the company has the option of constructing the portion of any drain, or drainage work required to be constructed upon, along, under or across the railway or lands.
Again, in layman's language, this subsection gives a railway company the option of carrying out the construction of a drain across its own right of way at its own expense. It is felt that a railway would prefer to do this in order to protect its own property.
Subsection (3) reads:
(3)	In the event of the company not exercising such option and completing such work within a reasonable time and without any unnecessary delay, such work may be constructed or completed in the same manner as any other portions of such work are provided under the laws of such province to be constructed.
Again, in layman's language, this subsection provides that if the railway company fails to exercise its option to carry out the construction of the drain across its own right of way within a reasonable time the drainage authority may do the work and charge the cost to the railway.
Subsection (4) states:
(4)	Notwithstanding anything in this section, no drainage works shall be constructed or reconstructed upon, along under or across the railway or lands of the company, until the character of such works, or the specification or plans thereof, have been first submitted to and approved by the board.
This subsection seems to provide the board of transport commissioners with a veto power over the specifications or plans for carrying a drain across the railway. If the drainage

National Energy Board Act authority drew up specifications or plans of an unreasonable nature the board of transport commissioners could compel them to revise the plans.
Even if section 273 were incorporated into the National Energy Board Act as is proposed this subsection (4) of section 273 of the Railway Act would provide the national energy board with a veto power over plans or specifications for carrying a drain across a pipe line right of way. Subsection (5) is very important to farmers and municipal drainage authorities. It reads as follows:
(5)	The proportion of the cost of the drain, or drainage works across or upon the railway to be borne by the company shall in all such cases, be based upon the increase of cost of such work caused by the construction and operation of the railway.
We have today in Middlesex county, the western part of which I represent, four major pipe lines crossing that area. One of them is operating under federal charter. Three of them are operating under provincial charters, and I wish to place on the record what this means to the local drainage authorities in that area. Archibald, Gray and McKay, drainage engineers of London, obtained this information from two pipe line companies, the Imperial Oil Company and the Sun (Canadian) Oil Company which operate two of the pipe lines across that area.
