Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege for me to be able to rise at this time to speak in support of the proposal which has been advanced by my colleague the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas) whose constituency is in the neighbourhood of my own. I know that the hon. gentleman has given this matter considerable study, thought and effort. I consider it a very important matter. There is perhaps no need of my rising to participate in this debate because our time is very limited and I therefore intend to take only a few moments to express my support of this measure. I did feel, however, that because I come from an area which I am sure is even lower and flatter than the area represented by my hon. friend I should make a few points at this time.
First of all I must say I am heartily in agreement with the hon. member's contention that tile underdrainage is essential to successful agricultural production in our part of southwestern Ontario. I feel I can safely say that we have many hundreds of miles of tile underdrainage in the part of southwestern Ontario I represent. Perhaps, therefore, I can speak with some authority on this matter. I have also had the privilege of serving in the municipal council of my municipality for 16 years. During that time we had many occasions to deal with municipal drainage both of the covered type which has been particularly referred to in the remarks of the hon. member who spoke previously and also considerable open drainage as well. There are thousands of acres in my part of the country that are low and flat to the point where the land has to be diked and pumped in order to take care of the extra water that falls in that area.
As a drainage contractor myself I have also had some experience in the laying of underdrainage. Because the land is so flat down there, and has so little variation, it is extremely important that accuracy be adhered to in the laying of those drains. There are parts of that country where there is a fall of a little more than 12 inches in a mile. That may seem strange to many people in 90205-6-49
National Energy Board Act this area who can look out their back windows and see hills that are perhaps hundreds of feet in height to think of a country where there is little more than 12 inches of fall to the mile, but that is so in parts of our area. Therefore, I should like to emphasize three points particularly. First, I feel that this bill which the hon. member for Middlesex West is asking the house to pass will be of considerable assistance to all types of underdrainings in instances where that drainage has been laid down previously to the laying of these pipelines. Where these pipelines do damage to those drains I feel that provision should be made in the legislation to make the company, or the board, as the case may be, that is responsible for the laying of these pipe lines responsible for the damage that they do to the underdrainage.
Second, by the same token, where open drainage is necessary as the hon. member for Middlesex West has explained, to carry water in places where so many underdrains have converged to the place where they create a sufficient volume of water that it is not economically possible to carry it away by underdrainage and therefore it becomes necessary to make open drains for a more free flow, I feel that where those pipelines interfere in any way with the free flow of those open drains then the pipe line should become responsible for the interference caused.
Where it is necessary to construct new drains as distinct from those that are laid after a pipe line has been laid I feel that, if, as a result of coming in contact with those pipe lines, it becomes necessary to increase the cost of this municipal drainage, or private drainage, as the case may be, the pipe line should be made responsible, or provision should be made in the law to make it responsible for the increased cost as a result of the pipe line being there.
These are the three main thoughts that I had in mind. I do appreciate the privilege that it is to speak for a few moments at this time and I would emphasize that I am heartily in accord with the proposal outlined by the hon. member for Middlesex West.

National Energy Board Act are not subject to the regulations of the provincial drainage scheme. I think this is a matter which should be corrected as soon as possible. I have not given this matter the same attention as the sponsor of the bill, but I think I can advance several practical reasons why oil companies, or oil pipe line companies, should not be subject to the same regulations as railway companies, public utilities and other bodies, at least in the province of Ontario, which I am speaking of at this time. I can see where surplus material left on the site after the pipe line was built could become a problem in so far as interfering with the drainage system is concerned. I can also visualize depressions caused by settlement. I know of a case of that kind where a depression caused a change in the drainage system, which in turn brought about a washout. This is an important matter.
I think another matter that should be taken into consideration is that of low lying properties, which have been mentioned, where drainage is slow and sluggish and drainage channels very quickly become grown up with weeds and brush and have to be cleaned out every two or three years; I think five years in some instances and three years in others. This is a rather expensive project. Generally, an engineering firm is brought in and makes a report on the estimated cost, and then the provincial drainage authority brings down a recommendation as to how the cost should be assessed. I think the pipe line companies which are crossing a piece of land of this type, using the land for getting the product from one place to another, should be definitely responsible for a part of the cost of keeping those waterways in a satisfactory condition.
There is also the question of trunk sewers and water mains, which affects municipalities perhaps more than other places. I have known of water mains which came in contact with a pipe line and there was a question of which one should go down. Should the water line go down or should the pipe line go down? If they came under provincial draining regulations these matters could be quite easily solved without any difficulty.
There is another matter that I doubt whether I can speak on at this time, but I know that there are others who might wish to speak on it. I might mention also the effect on field tile drainage systems. In the


riding that I represent the land is practically all under a field tile drainage system. We have at least a couple of oil pipe lines going through there and that also creates a problem because oil pipe lines are quite often close to the surface and they do interfere with drainage systems.

A pipe line, just the same as anything else that goes through the ground, disturbs the natural state of the land and does create problems. Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a word or two on the very important amendment to the National Energy Board Act introduced by the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas). I wish to compliment him on the great work he is doing for his own constituency and for southwestern Ontario in particular as far as this amendment is concerned.
For many years all of western Ontario has been trying to deal with this problem, first of all in connection with the railways and then in later years with respect to pipe lines. While there seems to be provision in the provincial act, as time goes by, we in that area and those in the Galt, Kitchener and Guelph areas will have to face the question of pipe lines for the distribution of water. Let us now make some changes in the act so that drainage installations, which are costly from the viewpoint of the farmer, are not made almost impossible.
The hon. member for Middlesex West pointed out the cost to the oil companies of lowering their pipe lines in accordance with provincial regulations, and if that cost is added to the cost of municipal tile drainage systems many of them will not be installed. Consequently it is of vital importance that the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Middlesex West be considered seriously at this time.
I also want to point out that for many years prior to 1903, when section 273 was

incorporated in the Railway Act, the railways hindered much of the development and drainage of those areas simply because they would not co-operate with the municipalities or with the farmers. With respect to the installation of pipe lines in Middlesex county over the past few years, if it had not been for the yeoman service of the Middlesex county federation of agriculture much greater difficulty would have been encountered. The oil companies were not too co-operative with respect to the expropriation of land and the restoration of tile drains.
Section 273, as I mentioned before, was incorporated in the Railway Act in 1903 to solve the problem and has served very well since that time. It is passing strange to me that when the National Energy Board Act was passed in order to deal with these problems the Railway Act was copied but section 273 of the Railway Act, strangely enough, was not included in the National Energy Board Act. It seems to me that it was more by design than by mistake that it was not incorporated in the act at the time.
I mentioned also that the question of water pipe lines may enter the picture in the years ahead. There is some reference to this in the Ontario act and I should like to read one portion of that act because to me it seems to leave some doubt whether water pipe lines would come under the provincial drainage laws. Section 20 of the Ontario act reads as follows:
Where a drainage work or a part of a drainage work is to be constructed, repaired, improved or maintained upon, along, adjoining, under or across the lands, permanent way, transmission lines, power lines, wires, conduits or other permanent property of a public utility, the public ' utility shall have the option of constructing, repairing, improving or maintaining such work or part.
So far as the distribution of water is concerned, in some cities this would be under the jurisdiction of a public utility but there is also the possibility that it might come under a conservation authority, which presents another problem to us and to the provincial authorities. It is interesting to note that the minister of highways of Ontario, Mr. Cass, has become very interested in this matter and, along with county councils, township councils and the Ontario federation of agriculture, has concurred in the proposed amendment introduced by the hon. member for Middlesex West. May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned at five o'clock, I was quoting some instances of corporations where the profit sharing theory is put into practice. I would have liked to quote some statistics to indicate the economic advantages which those companies reaped, but I shall spare you those figures. However, I do not want to omit the still greater advantages to the workers who participate in such plans, for they have been able in some cases to accumulate quite fabulous sums.
Thus, an employee of the Sears & Roebuck Company in the United States, who has 10 to 15 years of service, has, upon retirement, an average $11,106 in his pension fund; the man who has worked from 20 to 25 years gets an average of $48,024, and the one who has been from 30 to 35 years with the company gets $116,140. Finally, the man who has more than 35 years of service, gets the appreciable amount of $191,679.
In the case of the Motorola company, in Chicago, a worker who retired in 1959 after 12 years of profit sharing received a cheque for $16,618.
An employee of Signode Steed & Strapping, of Chicago had built up a fund of $39,506 after 19 years of sharing.
And now, Mr. Speaker, how can such a system be applied in the context of our present economy?
Should the government, by regulation, take the lead in implementing such a plan? I do not think so, as such an attitude would work against individual freedom. However, the government could play a truly constructive role by promoting friendly meetings between employers and workers and starting discussions towards that objective.
Under the circumstances, I think that the national productivity council, whose principles are now under consideration, is the very organization capable of looking carefully into our economic problems and the profit sharing schemes. The establishment of that body, long advocated by our distinguished leader, has been approved by trade unions and religious authorities.

Productivity Council
A second step that the government could and should take to promote closer co-operation between management and labour and a gradual change to profit sharing schemes would be to amend the Income Tax Act in order that contributions paid to a retirement fund would not be taxable.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, democracy itself is on trial today. Our friends in the group in the corner, and even the opposition in general, think we cannot pull ourselves out of this so-called hole that

we are in. We are not fully employed, as everybody knows, although a great many Canadians are still working. We have a national problem today, we have an international problem, and it is one and the same thing.
We believe that free men can work and will work. I think we can. But the problems are great and we have to have the knowledge. It is not enough to have dynamic leadership, and who will deny that we have that dynamic leadership in our Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker), in our cabinet and in the people who sit on this side of the house ready to back them up?
This is no piecemeal program. We have attacked this problem one stage at a time. We have stopped wasting the nation's money. We have spent money, all the money we had. Now we have to go back to work. The government is going back to work; we are at work behind them. Now I think it is time we asked the Canadian people to roll up their sleeves and get to work behind us and stop whining.
We believe in democracy, and this is one of the acceptances of that belief right here. This bill which has been introduced today asks the Canadian people to get together; it asks all five major groups to get together and take a good look at their problems, to stop theorizing and go back to work. There is no short cut to success, not even socialism. They work in the socialist countries, but they are not happy. If we go back to work here we can be happy; we can make a profit; we can show the free world that Canada is not only a great voice in the United Nations but a great voice at home in the factory and in the field.
One of the objects of this bill is to get us together, and I think it will. We are not sectional; we are not going to try to do it by organizing labour; we are going to try to do it by getting everybody together. Read clause 2 of the bill and you will see for yourselves. Our Prime Minister does not intend to be a dictator; he intends to be a chairman, a chairman of the Canadian people. I do not think this is a last ditch stand; I think the free world is going to win, and I make a personal appeal: I am willing to work. Are you?
If we get this council together it will not be enough. It is going to be a fact-finding organization; it is going to ask us what we know about our own business and then it is going to ask us what we are willing to do about it. You know what kind of an organization it is going to be. It is going to be a group of free Canadians putting their backs into it- leadership without compulsion.
I have heard a great deal of talk today that we cannot do it without compulsion. I do not believe it. The people up in my district are working, and people are willing
Productivity Council
to do more. All they ask from us is intelligent, planned leadership. We have shown it already, and we are going to show it again. I believe that such a source of information will provide more of what is needed than any other method of obtaining the answers to our present grave problems of how to obtain full employment. We have to talk straight to the people. We are not going to give them a Utopia without hard work. That is all I have to say at present.

Before we can do that, before we can compare the output per manhour in 1946 with that in 1959 we must reduce the dollar value to 1946 dollars, or reduce both to constant dollars. If that were done-and I have not

Productivity Council
been able to check the figures-I think we would find that over the past years our increase in manhour production has not gone up to any appreciable degree. To that extent we must, I think, increase our efficiency, particularly in the export industries. On the other hand, we must not lose sight of the fact that the more this bill contributes to the efficiency of industry the more it will contribute to unemployment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit one question? He mentioned earlier that the main purpose of the bill is to improve efficiency. Will the hon. member declare if he is for or against efficiency in industry?

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: If I thought the hon. member was going to ask a stupid question like that I would not have yielded the floor.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: I would like an answer.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I have already said I am supporting the principle of this bill. What more does the hon. member want? It is our duty over here to make constructive criticism, and that is what I am doing. Does the hon. gentleman himself deny that technical efficiency has made a contribution to our present unemployment? Does he deny that? I will give him a chance to answer when I sit down.
It seems to me that while the achievement of technical efficiency is one of our problems it is certainly not our most pressing problem. I would think that a body so broadly based as this proposed productivity council would be an appropriate body to serve two other purposes in addition to those outlined in the bill. One of those purposes could be, I think, the generation of some influence on the trend of productivity; to indicate to some degree the direction in which it should go in order to meet the needs of the people.
I admit that this would involve planning, but what I have in mind is not bureaucratic planning or state planning but voluntary planning by free men who take responsibility ' for the needs of the people as well as for the security and welfare of the nation and who, in order to do that, would be willing to work . together on a voluntary basis and plan to .make the best use of our resources. Industry was made for man, not man for industry. There are many urgent needs which are not being met by industry today simply because it is more profitable to meet other needs which are not so urgent.
I think the second purpose which this council could serve would be to act as a sort of watchdog over our resources. Our resources are not unlimited; they are not inexhaustible and they are not ours alone. We hold them in trust for future generations. As we look out today over the country and

see some of the products of industry I think it cannot be denied that in many ways our resources are being squandered. For example, we do not need all the big tail fenders that one sees on motorcars. The tendency to build in obsolescence is another way of squandering our resources. Then there is the manner in which technical improvements are doled out one year after another. We all know that many features which will appear on the 1965 cars are available today and that many features which will be incorporated in the 1965 television sets are available today. Yet industry does not see fit to make these improvements available because the practice has been built up of basing sales on styles which change year after year.
I hope the government will consider these two suggestions and make provision to include them in this bill among the objectives already listed so that this council when it is set up may be able to exert a positive influence on the direction productivity should take and at the same time utilize our resources to the maximum degree.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I have a few observations to make about the bill which is now before us. I must say that my impression when I saw the reference to this proposed legislation in the speech from the throne was a very favourable one. I imagined that what the government had in mind in making this proposal was what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) had had in mind in 1958 in the suggestion he put forward in the program which was advanced at that time when it was apparent that in addition to the unemployment which was caused by the recession at that time there was also the beginning of a good deal of structural unemployment caused by automation or what is usually considered automation today-technical advances of one kind and another.
I supposed that what the government had in mind was the setting up of a council which would primarily concern itself with what is, I think, a primary problem at the moment- that industry, in order to be competitive simply must advance technically and that in advancing it is apt, very often, indeed too often, to make many of its employees redundant. This creates problems unless there is sufficient growth in the economy at the same time to take up the slack in other industries. I would not question for one moment that the long term effects of automation will be advantageous just as the long term effects of what it is no longer fashionable to call the industrial revolution of the eighteenth century were advantageous.

Any historian knows that the short term effects were the exact reverse. They were to increase unemployment, and the unemployed on numerous occasions in rages broke the machines which they felt, were destroying their jobs. There are undoubtedly many unemployed persons today who feel the same kind of resentment at these advances which are throwing them out of work. Since this is the urgent and immediate problem, it seemed to me it was obviously the problem to which this council would address itself. I had all the more reason for thinking that because we know that the council was suggested at the end of a meeting which the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) called in October for the purpose of discussing unemployment. It was to a logical mind, I think, not unnatural to assume that this council that was produced out of a conference about unemployment would be primarily concerned with dealing with unemployment.
I must say it was quite a shock to me to read the bill this morning and find that it has no relationship whatever to the current and immediate unemployment problem. It was also somewhat of a shock to me when I examined the speech that was made on the resolution stage by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) to discover that several paragraphs of that speech which I can point out, if any hon. gentleman wishes me to, are simply taken absolutely verbatim but without any acknowledgement, from the memorandum submitted by the British productivity council to the select committee on estimates in the United Kingdom. Considering the fact that the hon. gentleman who introduced this resolution suggested to another hon. member earlier in this session that he should get a new speech writer it was something of a shock for me to discover that this distinguished minister of the crown who obviously glories in his own originality should have passed off as his own without any kind of acknowledgement several paragraphs from this document.
I am afraid that what the minister did in his speech is what the government is doing in the bill. Since there was no bill in the United Kingdom but merely a charter under the companies act-and I have not seen the charter so I am just inferring-it seems that this bill is as nearly as it can be a mirror or copy of that charter. I must say it looks like it.

speechtext: A copy of what?

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman had been following what I had been saying he would know that I had suggested it appears to be a copy of the charter of the British productivity council.
Productivity Council

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Has the hon. member seen it?

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Let us consider for a moment what the British productivity council was set up to do. It was set up at a time when there was over-full employment in the United Kingdom, when there was an acute labour shortage, when there was every need to economize in the use of labour and manpower in every possible way and when, moreover, the British who had suffered the terrible destruction and devastation they did suffer during the war were faced with the serious problem of getting their industries and particularly their export industry on a basis on which they could again compete in the world markets and restore something of the position they had enjoyed before the war.
It was, in other words, to deal with a problem which is the precise opposite of the immediate problem we have before us in this country at this time. That we also have a problem with respect to productivity I do not deny. I do not deny that it is necessary for some of the reasons the Prime Minister gave in moving second reading that we keep our industries modern and competitive. There is no doubt about that whatever, but I doubt whether Canadian industry is technically so backward and that the speed of automation has been so slow in this country that that is what one would call a really number one problem at this time. However, it is a genuine problem and for the reasons already given by my friends the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter), the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) and the hon. lady from Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh), who made such an effective maiden speech this afternoon, we feel this measure, to the extent that it is effective, will be dealing with a matter that is of national importance and ought to be supported. But we do not think it ought to be camouflaged as a measure to deal with the urgent unemployment problem, which we, unlike the government, regard as an economic emergency in this country at this time.
It seems to me it is additional evidence of the fact that appears to grow increasingly obvious that the government is primarily concerned about public relations and is only secondarily concerned about the actual effect of the measures it has introduced. I do not imagine that the idea of a productivity council was a child of the conference in October. It was something that the government had ready to be quickly pulled like a rabbit out of a hat so it would have something to put in the newspapers the next morning. To paraphrase from numerous speeches made in recent months by the right hon. gentleman who

Productivity Council
presides over the government-and I must paraphrase because I do not have the newspapers in front of me-this government has done so many good things and it has had no time to advertise them. I venture to say without any fear of successful contradiction that no government in the history of the world has done so little and advertised so much in the course of three years as this one has.
The stock in trade of hon. gentlemen opposite is words. That is the only commodity they seem at all capable of understanding. So far as I can judge one word seems to be just about as good as another for hon. gentlemen opposite, except one word which is a dirty word and must not be used, and that is the word "unemployment".
So far as the immediate problem of unemployment is concerned this measure cannot possibly make any kind of contribution whatever except to the extent that the appointment of 25 people and a few clerks and civil servants will perhaps provide a few part-time and possibly one or two full-time jobs, but whatever its long term effect on the economy may be its short term effect, based on the appreciation of it given to the house by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, its sponsor, the Prime Minister, its godfather, and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), its stepfather, will be negligible.
It seems to me it is about time that in these matters we did consider what things really mean and not what if one talks fast enough and incoherently enough they can be made to appear to mean for a very brief time. There is no one that is better at that than the right hon. gentleman who moved the second reading of this bill this afternoon.
I was also very much impressed by the speech made by the porte parole of the Prime Minister, his parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Martineau). Yesterday the hon. member for Pontiac told us that this productivity council was a very different thing from a body which was suggested by my hon. friend from Essex East (Mr. Martin) in an amendment which was moved to one of the motions to go into supply in the last session of parliament. What was the difference? What was the great difference that troubled the hon. gentleman constitutionally? The great difference was that what the hon. member for Essex East had suggested was a body which would advise the government and, forsooth, this government needs no advice from anybody. Therefore, a body that was to be advisory was ruled out; it was contrary to our British system of government, according to the hon. member

for Pontiac, the spokesman of the Prime Minister, and therefore we must be absolutely sure that any body that was set up would give no advice about policy, but it would advise once the policy had been set; it was then to give advice about administration. Some of us who have had some experience of government will find that doctrine quite extraordinary.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Don't be so modest.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
The notion that governments must not on any account receive any advice from outside their own ranks before it formulates policy, but must be advised about the administration, does seem to me to be a reversal of everything that is in the experience of those who have either had any experience of government or even have had much opportunity to observe government. It does seem to me that there is no question that any government and every government needs advice and it needs all the advice it can get and from the best possible sources. That was true of the previous government-I admit that at once-and it is certainly true of hon. gentlemen opposite.
If this productivity council is not being set up to advise the government, what on earth is it being set up to do? That is the question. If it is not to advise the government about policy, what is it to advise the government about? Surely it is not going into the individual businesses of individual concerns to tell the management how to run their businesses. If I understood the Prime Minister correctly, that would be socialism. If I understood one of the phrases he used this afternoon, that would be socialism. Surely it is not going to do that; surely it is going to be studying the general problems.
That does not mean that it is going to tell the government what to do; but it surely means that if it is going to be of any use it is going to provide advice, advice to industry, advice, perhaps, to the congress of labour and other trade unions who I think perhaps could do with a little also; but above all, advice to the Minister of Labour, to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and, indeed, to the government generally in helping them to formulate policies which, of course, it is their responsibility to do and their duty to do and which no one who believes in responsible government wants to take away from them. But surely it is no abrogation of the responsibility of the government to seek to get good advice, and I really cannot believe that the hon. member for Pontiac was correctly reflecting the views of the government when he made the statement.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: I rise on a question of privilege, because I certainly never said that the government should not seek advice. That is not what I said yesterday in the course of my speech on this matter. Following the interruption of the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate, I pointed that out. Why he should bring this up tonight, insisting and re-insisting that I said it, and misquoting me at length, I do not know.

speechtext: As it happens I have not attempted to quote the hon. gentleman at all, but since he asks me to quote him I do not mind doing so. All I did was to suggest what I had understood the hon. gentleman to say.

speechtext: Oh; that is different.

If one examines the motion made at that time by the hon. member for Essex East, it is quite apparent that there is no relation between it and the present productivity council, because that motion suggested that an advisory board be set up composed of different people:
"-for the purpose of developing economic policies designed to achieve a high and stable level of income and employment."

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Is that such a terrible thing?

speechtext:
I am going to read on:
In other words, that motion-

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Be fair.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
If I might be allowed to read the hon. gentleman's words unassisted by his friends, so that they will get clearly into Hansard, it would be better.
In other words, that motion would have had the effect, had it been accepted by this house, of substituting a policy-making body for the present government.
Of course, that statement itself is just nonsense, as was pointed out by my hon. friend from Ottawa West and by me. All it did was to suggest an advisory board; it did not suggest something to be substituted for the government at all.
Then, the hon. gentleman went on:
In other words, an advisory board to tell the government what policy it should adopt. I believe that under our democratic process it is up to the government that has the confidence of the people-
At that point there was an interjection "More or less". If I had been making the interjection I would have left out the first two words. I continue:
Productivity Council
I believe that under our democratic process it is up to the government that has the confidence of the people to produce policies and then,-
This is the doctrine, sir:
-if it is necessary to establish different boards or different advisory bodies to put the policy into effect,-
Well, now, I did not-

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Continue.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
-ever hear of having an advisory board to put a policy into effect. Surely you have an advisory board to help you generate a policy. Having generated a policy, you then put it into effect as an executive act. However, the hon. member is going to have an advisory board to put the policy into effect; after, as he says, the government makes it. I continue:
This is the purpose of the present resolution.
When the policies have been generated by this all-wise government then this productivity council will put them into effect-I do not want to denature the hon. gentleman's words-if it is necessary. This is what he said:
-to produce policies and then, if it is necessary to establish different boards or different advisory bodies to put the policy into effect, of course the government sees to it.
Therefore, what this advisory productivity council is intended to do, according to the hon. member for Pontiac, is to put the policies into effect that the government has generated. As I say, sir, it was really so extraordinary a doctrine about responsible government that it did seem to me it should not pass entirely unnoticed. I know that the Prime Minister has pointed out before now that parliamentary secretaries are not members of the government and therefore I feel it is not fair to ask the government to take the responsibility for what the hon. member said. I am not doing that but I do think the Prime Minister ought to tell us, in view of this rather astonishing doctrine, precisely what he thinks the productivity council is really going to do and how it is going to do it, in simple, clear, coherent language and not in involved hyperbole, which is rather more characteristic of some of the explanations we get at times about these measures.
There are just two other observations I wish to make. This bill is the fourth of four measures that were introduced at the very outset of the session as the government's pre-Christmas program to deal with the problem of unemployment. The first measure was the amendment to the National Housing Act, and I think every one of us hopes that those amendments will work really well. There were some of us who were rather troubled and are

Productivity Council
still rather troubled about some of the restrictions that there seemed to be upon them, particularly upon one of them, but I am not going to transgress the rules by going into that. The extent to which this housing legislation will provide additional employment depends upon the extent to which it is used and I for one, and I think I can speak for every member on this side of the house, hope that it works exceedingly well and produces a great many jobs. At any rate, no one would question that it could have some relatively immediate effects.
The second measure was the bill respecting loans to small business. It was rather hard to tell whether that was really meant to aid small business or really meant to produce employment. I do not say that the two are exclusive but I have some very grave doubts about its immediate, though not its ultimate, employment generating possibilities.
The third bill was the one we disposed of yesterday, the vocational training measure, which was not as good as we would like to see but nevertheless was a fairly good measure. I said before and I say again that it was a fairly good bill and marks a considerable advance but it is not going to provide, apart from the advisory council that has been set up, one job immediately. In a few months it may provide some jobs on the building of schools but those schools will have to be planned, organized and started before the measure will provide any jobs that would not have been provided anyway because of the assistance to be given to schools already under construction or already planned. Therefore, of these three measures the only one that will provide any immediate additional employment at all is the one amending the National Housing Act.
This is the fourth measure to come before us, and if the Prime Minister can show any way in which it is going to provide any immediate employment I am sure we will all be very pleased and I will certainly take back anything of this sort I have said. I cannot find anything in the bill that would justify any immediate hopes of that kind.
It will be recalled that on September 21 the Prime Minister made a speech on television in which he admitted for the first time that there was some unemployment in this country, in which he told the unemployed that they were really unemployed. But he also told us in that speech on September 21 that the government had a lot of plans that were ready in detail to be submitted to parliament. I think it can be shown that the housing act was not one of them because at that time the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker), who is responsible for housing, was making rather different kinds of noises about

housing. It is quite clear that the things contained in the housing act amendments had not been generated in the government in September and had not yet reached the point of policy and, as I have shown, none of the other measures is going to provide any immediate employment.
So I think it is about time that the Prime Minister told us what those measures were that were ready in detail in September to be submitted to parliament because so far we have had none of them in this session. I admit that perhaps this is not strictly relevant to the second reading of the bill but in my opinion it has some relevancy. And I invite the Prime Minister when he gets up to conclude the debate to show us precisely in what way the measure now before the house is going to provide any additional jobs in the next six months.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words must be of appreciation to several hon. members who in the course of the debate this afternoon made a contribution to the discussion of the problem that we are endeavouring to meet through the formulation of this legislation. I should like particularly to say to the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Miss La-Marsh) that I am sure the house listened to her contribution with interest and, if I may, I convey to her my congratulations. I listened to her most carefully. I am of those who through the years have always been most happy to see new members come into the house and make, in the course of their maiden speeches to the house, that type of contribution that is in keeping with the best traditions of the house. For her I express the sincere hope that during her period of service in parliament she will continue to make a contribution to the solution of those problems that all of us face. I know something of what a trying experience a maiden speech is. All of us have gone through that. I recall with trepidation even at this date the excruciating experience through which I passed for several days in advance of the ordeal.
In paying my tribute to her may I say, however, that with respect to her description of Niagara Falls as an economic desolation, or so I understood her words to convey, it was of interest that while she was speaking I had before me an excerpt from the Niagara Falls Review of Friday or Saturday last. I am sure she would want me to see that the record is complete by quoting the words expressed at that time by William R. Sootheran,

chairman of the greater Niagara industrial committee. He is reported as follows:
One of the most productive years in this area's history of industrial growth has been recorded in 1960, William R. Sootheran, chairman of the greater Niagara industrial committee, told members of the Niagara Falls, Stamford and Chippawa municipal councils Friday.
"A total of six new firms have settled in the area and eight local industries have made major expansions to their manufacturing facilities," Mr. Sootheran said ...
Mr. Sootheran also expressed confidence that in the coming year "industrial growth will continue to expand due to the greater Niagara industrial committee's efforts," . . .
"The first firm to announce its intention of opening a new plant in the Niagara area was the Ford Motor Company of Canada Limited. When finished in early 1961, the 125,000-sq.ft. factory will employ approximately 250 persons," Mr, Sootheran continued.
"Then came Canadian Ohio Brass Company Limited with their plans to house the Holan division which will manufacture specialized truck bodies. This plant will also be in operation early in the new year."
Sterilon of Canada Limited, a subsidiary of Buffalo's Sterilon Corporation, has located here in a modern plant. . . and they are in full production at the present time,,-
And so on it goes. He said Anally as follows:
It has been an active year and great progress has been made in promoting the advantages of Niagara Falls as a site for new industry.
I thought those words of this industrial official might And their place in Hansard as well.
To the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) I should like to say that I always listen to his remarks with great attention. I think he is becoming somewhat lonely though. He is still an unreconstructed socialist. He has not allowed the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Pitman), by the process of political osmosis, to change him, even although they are quite closely allied at the moment, I am sure he will view with alarm the early departure from the name of his party through the assumption by the same old party of a new name in which private enterprise, according to the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), is going to play a large and important part. These are indeed the days of transition. I only hope that the hon. gentleman will be able to And that solace and satisfaction in the old party with the private enterprise features and new phases that some others sitting close to him now And themselves able to appreciate.
In the course of his remarks the hon. member mentioned one or two points. He spoke most disparagingly of private enterprise. Of course he was not in Calgary last week, Mr. Speaker. That must have been a meeting that gathered together the hon.
90205-6-50i
Productivity Council
member for Assiniboia and others. The hon., member for Assiniboia spoke there feelingly and touchingly about the effects of private enterprise. That was not the position taken by the hon. member for Kootenay West. He made quite clear today what he thought with regard to the policies that were necessary for Canada, namely the maintenance of socialism in all its strength and power.
He asked the reason-and it was a perfectly proper question-why this institution was described as a charitable organization. I put it simply to him that the reason for that description is that if donations are made to charitable institutions, the donors are permitted to make the necessary deductions when determining the amount of their liability for income tax. Any corporations that make a contribution to the strengthening or to the improvement of the institution or to the fund in general of the productivity council will be able thereby, by reason of this clause, to claim the necessary deductions when determining income tax liability.
As to the manner in which jobs will be provided, I now come to one of the most interesting speeches that have been made. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) is always interesting. He spoke as an historian. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that he emphasized the fact that historians have certain knowledge and certain information that is denied to the rest of us. I found that fact singularly interesting because he is an historian. There have been some who have stated, and with some cause, that his latest contribution to the history of one of my predecessors may well win him the fiction award for 1960.
I must say this, Mr. Speaker. When he spoke of the fact that the legislation that has been brought before the house at this time will not provide jobs, let me point out that the legislation passed yesterday, almost as soon as third reading had been given to that legislation, permitted the following announcement to be made today, namely the construction of a new building for the eastern Ontario institute of technology, Ottawa.
It will cost about $2 million. Final plans have not been completed, but the building is to be pushed forward, immediately, ...
It will be constructed under the federal-provincial emergency program under which the federal government pays 75 per cent of the capital costs of buildings for technical education.
That is No. 1. All across this nation, as a result of one other piece of legislation that provided for a contribution from the federal government in connection with pollution measures, the result has been a tremendous demand everywhere in Canada by

Productivity Council
municipalities to take advantage of the legislation passed by this parliament to the end that if the work is done before March 31, 1963 the federal government provides a 25 per cent bonus of the amount of the loan advance. Everywhere across the country towns and municipalities are making applications to the end that they may proceed at once, because we fixed a date close enough and yet far enough away, to permit of the plans being made and the provisions being taken forthwith so that jobs would be maintained and employment would be increased.
To the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate I say this. If he had listened this afternoon to the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Best), he would have had an answer to the question he raised during the course of his remarks this evening. To the hon. member for Halton I want to say that his speech today was one of those to be remembered in this house, being representative of study, personal knowledge and experience. A reading of that speech will answer the questions of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate as clearly as it was enunciated as to the purposes of the legislation; and no further words on my part are required in order to explain the legislation.
I must say that I followed with considerable interest the philosophical discourse of the hon. gentleman. He spoke of the ideas of the opposition, their clear-cut conception of what is to be done. They have never revealed it in the house, but they have it, Mr. Speaker.
But do you not recall that a few months ago a meeting was convened at Queen's University. There, from all parts of Canada, gathered together as of old in the cave of Adullam, were the representatives of liberalism with a small "1". There were mighty few of them from over there, because there were only six or seven chosen of the two hundred. They went there. When the hon. gentleman says they have an answer to these problems, the period of office from 1936 to 1940 and unemployment at that time, before the days of automation, is an answer to many of their arguments of today when they say they have an answer.
But they met. They were gathered there by selection and by choice. The viewpoints were all types of viewpoints. I have read them. It is a magnificent study in confusion. Read over the various concepts that were produced there. There were those that ranged from the official viewpoint of the Liberal party, which bear the Lamontagne trademark, to the economic fringe group. They were far to the left. One advocated the welfare state, financed by a tax on advertising.
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
I have not the record here. I have sent out for some of the clippings. Then there was the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). He said, "What Canada should have is a Canadian identity". Then there was the other group which believed in complete integration with the United States. Then there were those, Mr. Speaker, who when they were dealing with this great problem of employment said, "What we must do is to assure that Canadian industry shall have a Canadian identity".
At the same time the president of the Liberal federation, one of the major shareholders in an insurance company, sold out that company to the United States because it had a provincial licence. It was a gathering of the clans and the objective was to meet the problem of unemployment and to assure full production in Canada.
Then there were the old boys, many of them who said that what we require is a greater degree of centralization. Those were the autocrats of those days. Then there were the free traders. I spoke of the cave of Adullam that brought together all with varying thoughts. There was the free trade group, with Walter Gordon, the political boss of the Liberal party, as its chief opponent. It was most interesting that on the question of employment, how to meet the problem of automation, there was even more confusion than in the general concepts of the party.
Then there was the defence group, headed by a professor who advocated that in the interests of peace the Soviet defence minister, Mr. Malinovsky, should attend the meetings of the Canadian cabinet defence committee. That was one of the great conferences of all time.
Finally-and with this I must say I am not in disagreement-Michael Barkway in his analysis claimed he had heard remarks that the Liberals "cannot win public confidence unless they become completely disassociated from the old regime". No matter what we may think of those words, he ended up with these words and I bring them out because of the observation made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate respecting the confidence the people of Canada have in this government. Mr. Barkway said this:
It would be a ghoulish task to try to catalogue the dismal illusions and failures of the later Liberal years.
I want to give the whole quotation:
They would fill a book-a history of the 1950's which badly needs to be written.
I commend to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, when he finishes his present monumental work, that he might be able to undertake that work to which Mr. Barkway refers.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: I intend to.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
If the hon. member intends to do that, I hope he keeps closer to the facts. Then Mr. Barkway says:
But for the present purpose it is vital to indicate four of them which hang like millstones around the party's neck.
I thought I ought to refer to that conference. I looked through the references, the speeches and the deliberations and, sir, if you can find anything on this problem in which the two hundred were in agreement, then indeed you will have discovered something that I was unable to find.
The problem is a difficult one. The problem of unemployment today in all parts of North America is one that affects the thinking of the very best in public life, in industry, in economics, in the field of labour. All are endeavouring to arrive at something that will bring about a solution of a problem difficult, as the hon. member mentioned, in its implications and difficult to be met completely at an early date.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate has mentioned that on September 21 I referred to the program. We have been placing it before parliament step by step since this session began, and we intend to continue.
I did not intend to bring the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) in but I read from Hansard that in the resolution stage he complained, with great sincerity, of the fact that government members were daring to speak: they should not do that. He criticized that. He said, "They are holding up the legislation". It is only about three months ago that he was complaining that they were not speaking. On the one hand, in the last session of parliament the complaint was that they were not discharging their responsibilities; they were not speaking, and now the complaint is that, they analyse and assess and have taken the place of the opposition.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: It will not be long.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Now they are criticized, in return-

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: You are getting them trained for it.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not want to engage in any training of the hon. gentlemen, though I may have to. But I want to say this. They have criticized each piece of legislation. They have said it would not be effective. Then, Mr. Speaker, when the vote is called they are always there. Oh, it has been an interesting study as we watch them. Yet point after point is brought forward, and the legislative
Productivity Council
program is just nicely under way. Much remains to be introduced. It is difficult for the opposition. They do not feel very happy about it.
The members who support the government are attempting to present something of Canada's position. They are not being overly optimistic. They are able to point at an increase in production, at the greatest export trade in our history; they are able to point at a greater number of men employed than ever before, the same situation as exists in the United States. On the other hand, they are also trying to make their contribution to meet this problem which all of us are endeavouring to meet. The reason hon. gentlemen opposite are feeling not as happy as they were feeling a few months ago is the fact that they are finding that their policy of gloom, always gloom, is proving less and less effective among more and more people. They see a rising national production; they see a rising agricultural production, a greater and better return for agriculture, an increase in manufacture and production; they see the greatest trade with the United Kingdom that has ever taken place in our country; they see all of these things at a time of intense international competition. And they do not seem to be too happy about the results in that regard.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister a question?

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
When I am finished I shall be very glad to hear the question.
I simply say this: this is one more of the pieces of legislation. We do not say it will effect wonders but it is a major step forward. Placed alongside the steps already taken and those yet to be taken we believe we have outlined a plan which will give to Canadians as a whole new hope and new opportunities. Now, what is the question?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister this: will he put on the order paper between now and the time we adjourn for the Christmas recess the steps he intends to take over and above those he has already announced to deal with the emergency and the unemployment situation in the country today?

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
We shall place on the order paper, in accordance with the regular plan, the steps we intend to take, but we are not going to be stampeded into following the suggestions of the opposition in that regard. On the order paper, I believe tonight or tomorrow, will appear the step in agriculture. Then there are further steps which will be outlined as legislation is passed after full and complete discussion. Finally, just before the end of the session, prior to the Christmas

Division
holidays, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) will produce what has been described as a baby budget, and I want to say in that connection that the hon. gentleman will have every opportunity of discussing it before the Christmas adjournment. They raised an objection to the fact that the date fixed is December 20. The reason for that date is the absence of ministers on their duties in Europe.
The other day it was stated there was something about this that was unfair and unjust. Do hon: gentlemen opposite remember 1952? At that time, when they sat over here, they introduced the budget just before Easter, one day before the adjournment, and it went over without discussion until after the Easter holidays. Do they recall 1955 when the same course was followed? We shall place before the house, as I said before, further legislation, further legislative steps. We have yet, of course, to face the house on the question of the supplementary estimates. We should like to get these through before Christmas. As soon as we have the present items of legislation passed we shall proceed in the order indicated by the leader of the house. Having done that, we shall be in a position to carry out further legislative enactments. The course of action is ready. The chart has been laid out.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Bring it on.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: I respect the curiosity of the hon. gentleman, because each of these pieces of legislation they say is worthless, and then they vote for it. We are going to bring on further matters, and ultimately the whole picture will be here to receive the attention of the House of Commons. But we are not going to throw legislation at the house in an indiscriminate manner. We intend to follow a regular and proper plan to the end that the house and parliament as a whole may have the opportunity to fully consider all these matters, and we believe that out of this general plan, when finally it finds its way to the statute books, we shall have gone a long way toward carrying out those promises which we made in 1957 and 1958 in their entirety, and that we shall also have gone a long way to bring about that degree of economic prosperity which is the objective of this government.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Before clause 1 carries I should like to draw attention to the fact that-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: The hon. member for York Centre has the floor.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Since the whip has made an observation, I think I should draw your attention to the fact that, unless the minister speaks, it has always been the custom in this house, in my experience, to recognize a member of the opposition. If the minister wishes to speak I will yield to him at once.
As I was saying, I merely rose to draw attention to the fact that in the exceedingly entertaining and utterly irrelevant speech that the Prime Minister made on the second reading he was most careful not to answer the question that perhaps I should have asked in committee anyway rather than on second reading; and the question I repeat to the stepfather of the bill who is now sponsoring it in committee is, will the minister tell us just how many jobs this bill is going to provide in the next six months? This is the question I invited the Prime Minister to answer; this is the question he ignored completely. I would also ask the minister to tell us at the same time just what procedure he envisages will be followed under this measure to provide jobs over a longer period, and how many additional jobs will be generated by this legislation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Why not ask the hon. member for Laurier? He knows everything.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: This is government legislation.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
With respect to the inquiry of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate as to how many jobs the setting up of the productivity council will create, that is certainly a nonsensical question because the council is being set up to delve into the industrial sector in co-operation with management and
Productivity Council
labour committees now established to the extent of 1,600 across the country in order to find out where and how productivity can best be increased. At the same time it will have in mind the human element in the industry concerned and try to work out a plan whereby people who may be displaced because of automation can find some other useful place in our economy.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: The minister's answer is fine as far as it goes but it does not go very far. The minister talks about looking after the human element. As I said earlier at another stage of the bill, it was precisely the human element in the problem that those of us on this side of the house expected this council would be primarily concerned with. The urgent problem at this time is to provide jobs for the people who have already been displaced by measures to increase productivity. I think the minister should tell us just how the council is going to deal with the human element and what techniques the government envisages it will use to deal with what the minister referred to as persons displaced by measures to increase productivity. That is what we really want to know. That is the crucial question with respect to the bill and the one on which I should like to hear the minister.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: When automation sets in in any industry there are no provisions under present circumstances, unless there is a humane feeling on the part of those controlling the industry itself, to enable the people who are displaced to re-establish themselves when as a result of automation or technological change they find themselves out of a job. The ultimate and most important job of the productivity council will be, if automation is resorted to in an industry in order to accelerate productivity, to recommend the retraining of the people who are displaced so that they may be best fitted into some other useful employment in our labour force.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Following the answer given by the minister, I take it it would not be the job of the council to recommend policies that might help to provide alternative employment for those persons who have lost their jobs. Is that right?

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: No, not specifically.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Then there seems to be a misapprehension about the whole legislation. As was mentioned in the debate on earlier stages of the bill, it was announced by the Prime Minister at the conclusion of a conference on unemployment-I do not have the clippings here but this is the gist of it-that the council would help to do something to meet the problem of unemployment. In any

Productivity Council
event, the establishment of the council was announced, in conjunction with the report on the conference on unemployment. The legislation is mentioned in the speech from the throne and reference is made there to the ultimate success of efforts to improve Canada's trade and employment. What I should like the minister to do now is to relate to the committee a little more closely just how this measure will improve the employment situation in Canada. I would ask him to relate that in a more specific way bearing in mind the genesis of the legislation and the way in which it was announced and, if you like, represented to the public.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: The conference that was called in October by the Prime Minister was not a conference on unemployment. I think the hon. member should note that it was a conference on employment. In my view the best way that the productivity council can assist in the matter of employment is by helping to make industry in this country more efficient and as a result more competitive. Consequently, because of the improved ability of industry to sell its products abroad more employment would be created.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Because of the remarks which the Minister of Labour has made in answer to questions already put to him by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and the hon. member for Ottawa West it seems to me that this is a measure which should be under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Labour, and I am wondering why the government decided to put it under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Would the minister explain that to the committee?

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: It actually comes under both. Reports will be made to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Labour but because of the fact that productivity is involved and as a result the exporting of products it properly comes under the Minister of Trade and Commerce who will report to parliament.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Is it not primarily a matter falling under the jurisdiction of labour rather than trade and commerce?

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext: Not primarily, no. It is a cooperative effort, we hope, on the part of labour, management and other groups and that is why the composition of the productivity council is as set out in the bill.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am wondering why the Liberal opposition voted for the bill tonight in view of the questions they have asked. They are asking the same questions that I asked. Why do we need a productivity council in Canada when, as was indicated in most of the speeches made today, we are overproducing in almost every field. Unless we can get rid of the products we have now we are one of the last countries in the world to need a productivity council. We need a sales council. We need to put all our efforts into selling the products we now produce. In each of the fields where productivity has been speeded up we have a surplus. May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman?
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask what we will be doing tomorrow and Thursday?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, Thursday will be a government day and the private members' Thursday will be postponed to a future date. We have before us now the productivity council bill in the committee stage. I also suggested that we would consider supplementary estimates and if we finish the productivity bill tomorrow we will take up supplementary estimates. In addition to those two items, we have the resolution on veterans pensions which was introduced last night and in Votes and Proceedings tomorrow will appear a resolution dealing with a proposed agricultural program. I presume that these four items will take up the time of the house on Wednesday, Thursday and Friday. If there is any change in the order of consideration it will be announced at the appropriate time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I take it then that if we complete the productivity council legislation tomorrow we' will go on with the supplementary estimates and continue with them until completed.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It depends on the progress we make. Each evening I will suggest to the house what we will continue with but tomorrow, being a short day, I would expect that we would not get very far with the supplementary estimates and might have to carry on with them oh Thursday.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
